Why India’s go-to Russian oil imports are set to fall & Brazilian supplies may quadruple in November

The November figures are based on trends and estimates up to 15 November and may change when full-month import data becomes available.

New Delhi: India’s Russian crude imports are projected to fall by nearly 400,000 barrels per day (b/d) in November, while purchases from Brazil are expected to almost quadruple, pointing to a shift in the country’s oil sourcing as changing prices make alternative supplies more attractive to refiners.

India’s overall crude imports are estimated to average around2 5.2 million b/d in November, compared with a record 5.7 million b/d in October, according to preliminary Kpler data shared by Natalia Katona, a commodity analyst with OilPrice.com based in Abu Dhabi. Higher purchases from Saudi Arabia and Iraq have also helped offset the decline in Russian supplies.

However, the moderation in imports does not necessarily indicate weaker refinery demand. Katona said October’s unusually high purchases should be taken into account when assessing the November figures, rather than viewing the moderation as an indication of a slowdown in refining activity.

Show Full Article

The more significant development is the changing composition of India’s crude imports.

Russian deliveries are projected at around 1.7 million b/d in November, down from approximately 2.07 million b/d in October. This follows a sharp increase observed earlier in the year, when Russian supplies accounted for more than half of India’s crude imports in July, according to Kpler data.

The November figures are based on trends and estimates up to 15 November and may change when full-month import data becomes available.

The latest decline is primarily linked to pricing rather than any fundamental shift in India’s preference for Russian oil.

Russian Urals crude is generally priced against Dated Brent, a benchmark reflecting the price of physical crude oil cargoes, with sellers offering an additional premium or discount depending on market conditions.

During October, Dated Brent surged to $120-135 per barrel, around $18-20 above Dubai and ICE Brent, amid physical crude shortages in Northern Europe. ICE Brent is an international crude oil benchmark based on futures contracts traded on the Intercontinental Exchange and is widely used to price oil purchases globally.

However, Russian sellers were slow to adjust Urals pricing to reflect these changes, Katona said. Urals was offered at a premium of around $7 per barrel to Dated Brent at the beginning of October, with prices remaining at or above the benchmark until early November. This made Russian crude more expensive than competing grades for Indian refiners.

Russian discounts return, Gulf and Brazilian supplies gain The pricing situation has since changed. Russian producers have begun offering Urals at a discount of around $3-4 per barrel to Dated Brent in November, which itself has fallen to around $96 per barrel. Its premium over Dubai has also narrowed to approximately $4 per barrel.

This has made Russian crude more attractive to Indian refiners, and Katona expects them to increase their orders for December deliveries.

“Russian producers have clearly adjusted to regional pricing and are once again making Urals economically attractive, although the effect will show up in deliveries over the coming months,” she said.

Other factors could also support Russian exports to India. Fewer Russian refineries were offline in October as Ukrainian attacks eased, allowing more crude to be processed domestically.

However, the seasonal closure of the Northern Sea Route is expected to reduce the volume of Russian crude moving to China through that route, potentially freeing up more supplies for India. Katona expects this to support higher Urals deliveries to India in December and January.

Meanwhile, imports from the Middle East Gulf are increasing, particularly from Saudi Arabia and Iraq.

Saudi Arabia has stepped up exports from its Gulf terminals as its Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu faces repeated Houthi attacks. This has made India an attractive destination for Saudi sellers because of its proximity to Gulf export terminals, reducing voyage times and freight costs, Katona said.

The same economics apply to Iraqi crude. Katona expects the price difference between Gulf crude grades and Dubai to narrow for December deliveries as shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz improves and regional oil producers restore output.

Meanwhile, Brazil has emerged as another important supplier, with India’s imports of Brazilian crude projected to reach around 400,000 b/d in November, almost four times October’s level of around 100,000 b/d. Meanwhile, Venezuelan crude supplies to India are estimated to remain steady at around 300,000 b/d during the month.

The increase in Brazilian supplies comes as the country’s oil production reaches record levels following the ramp-up of new projects. At the same time, Chinese buyers have reduced their purchases of Brazilian crude, creating an opportunity for Indian refiners to secure cargoes.

Another advantage is that Brazilian and Venezuelan oil shipments do not have to pass through conflict-hit regions or vulnerable shipping routes, making them relatively more secure supply options for Indian refiners.

(Edited by Anupama Yadav)
